analysis.one_liner: Ends federal subsidies, tax breaks, and royalty relief for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stripped away a long list of federal favors for fossil fuel companies: it repealed royalty relief for offshore oil and gas drilling, raised the minimum royalty companies pay on federal coal, oil, and gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, ended more than a dozen tax breaks for oil, gas, and coal producers, shut down the Energy Department's fossil fuel research office, barred federal agencies and the World Bank from financing coal and oil projects, removed the legal cap on oil companies' liability for offshore and pipeline spills, and imposed a new 13% tax on oil and gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by one independent senator and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop paying for subsidies the bill's own findings put at over $72 billion between 2002 and 2008 while the five largest oil companies made over $1 billion (the text says $1,000,000,000) in profits in the prior decade [S3]. People living near coal trains, ports, and pipelines would gain from stricter spill liability, and communities hit by oil spills would no longer have their losses capped at a fixed amount [S2] [S3]. Renewable energy would compete on a level field after decades of larger federal investment in fossil fuels [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, spill victims, and coastal communities

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Interior Secretary's authority to reduce or eliminate royalty payments on offshore oil and gas leases and ends shallow-water and deepwater Gulf royalty relief programs, so companies pay the public for what they extract [S2] [S3].
Raises minimum federal royalties on coal, oil, and natural gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, increasing public revenue from resources owned by all Americans [S3].

Terminates more than a dozen tax provisions that lower oil, gas, and coal companies' taxes, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost expensing, and the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil, gas, and coal [S3].

Eliminates the cap on offshore facility and pipeline operators' spill liability and denies tax deductions for spill cleanup and damages, so companies rather than taxpayers and affected communities absorb spill costs [S3].

Stops the World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, the Department of Transportation, and the Rural Utilities Service from funding coal, oil, or natural gas projects, and terminates the DOE Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies would lose the subsidies, tax preferences, below-market royalties, and liability caps the bill repeals; consumers could see some of the higher royalties and the new 13% Gulf severance tax passed through in fuel prices, and communities dependent on fossil fuel extraction and transport jobs could face economic losses.

drawbacks.text: Some costs would reach consumers: the higher 18.75% royalties and the new 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico oil and gas extraction are levied on producers, who can pass part of them through to prices at the pump and on utility bills [S3].

The bill terminates not only subsidies but also federal fossil energy research and loan guarantee authority, including for advanced fossil technologies and carbon capture, which supporters of those programs argue could slow cleaner technologies that still depend on fossil infrastructure during a transition [S2] [S3].

Ending LIFO inventory accounting and other tax provisions would raise taxes on some smaller independent producers and coal mining regions, not just the five large oil corporations the bill's findings target [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is ending direct transfers and tax preferences to highly profitable companies, which most independent analyses value in the tens of billions over time, and making polluters bear more of their own spill costs. The honest tradeoffs are real but narrower: modest pass-through of higher royalties and the Gulf tax into fuel prices, job losses in coal-dependent regions, and the loss of federal research support for technologies like carbon capture that some see as part of a transition. On balance the costs fall mostly on the industry the bill targets, with some spillover to consumers and fossil-dependent communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2012 on May 10, 2012; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, natural gas, and coal companies kept the subsidies, tax preferences, below-market royalties, and capped spill liability the bill would have ended — subsidies the bill's own text valued at over $72 billion over 2002-2008, alongside over $1 billion in profits by the five largest oil corporations in the prior decade [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies kept their subsidies

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 10, 2012 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no party breakdown exists; the lone sponsor was an independent senator and no Democrat or Republican signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill repeals their offshore royalty relief, raises their federal lease royalties from 12.5% to 18.75%, ends over a dozen tax preferences, and imposes a 13% Gulf severance tax. These are direct public subsidies and below-market terms the companies currently receive from the government.

Royalty rates on federal coal leases rise from 12.5% to 18.75%, percentage depletion and coal royalty capital gains treatment end, and federal agencies are barred from financing coal projects at home and abroad.
The bill removes the statutory liability cap for offshore and pipeline oil spills, so companies would pay more of the true cost of spills instead of taxpayers and coastal communities.

industries.industry: Export credit and international finance (Ex-Im Bank, OPIC, World Bank recipients)
industries.note: Federal export and development financing for foreign coal and oil projects would be rescinded and prohibited, ending publicly backed support for fossil fuel projects overseas.

industries.industry: Rail and port operators hauling coal, oil, and gas
industries.note: Department of Transportation grants, loans, and guarantees could no longer fund rail or port projects for fossil fuel transport.

Removing decades of larger federal support for fossil fuels would level the competitive field; the bill's findings note $72 billion in fossil subsidies versus $12.2 billion for renewables from 2002 to 2008.
